O15:AB15 and VBA Module1 (`OverrideETSFast`, `SolveFast`). Row numbers are legacy rows. Formulas not stored in the
dump are inferred from the row labels and cached values and marked *(inferred)*.

**Inputs.**

| Rows | Item |
|---|---|
| 1800-1809 | Apply ETS; cap change at start and target (% vs baseline); cap continuation; start and target years; auction proportion at start and target; continuation; override switch |
| 1811-1813 | Risk premium inputs: price volatility 0.42, impact 0.5, policy risk 0.2 |
| 1815-1836 | Sector table: included flag, baseline emissions, semi-elasticity of emissions to the carbon price (power −0.00279, transport −0.00283, residential −0.00386, industry −0.00549, CBAM −0.001 per USD per t), generic proportions |
| 1843 | Relative price of an auctioned ETS against a tax for the same emissions target: 1.1 |
| 1846-1847 | Relative effectiveness, hardcoded: auctioning 1.0, output-based allocation (OBA/OBR) 0.5 |

Allocation is one time path of the auctioned share $a$ (rows 1863-1864; OBA share $1 - a$), the same for every
covered sector.

**Fast estimate (no iteration).**

1. Covered semi-elasticity (row 1845): coverage-weighted average of the sector semi-elasticities, $\varepsilon$ =
   −0.00288 in the cached run. The all-sector average used for the carbon tax (row 1844) is −0.00371.
2. Reduction left for the ETS (rows 1858-1860): the reduction the cap needs minus that of other policies, counted
   as an effective carbon price times $\varepsilon_{tax}$ (row 1859; for example 50 USD per t $\times$ −0.00371 =
   −18.6%).
3. Effectiveness of the allocation mix (row 1866): $e = a \times 1.0 + (1 - a) \times 0.5$.
4. Adjusted semi-elasticity (row 1867): $\varepsilon_{adj} = \varepsilon\, e$. With full OBA,
   −0.00288 $\times$ 0.5 = −0.00144, matching the cached value.
5. Estimated price (row 1868, `QuickEstimateOfETSPrices`): $p \approx$ (reduction left for the ETS) /
   $\varepsilon_{adj}$ *(inferred: linear semi-elasticity form)*.

This closed-form estimate ignores the full fuel-demand model, where the response comes from prices and elasticities
by fuel and subsector, not from one semi-elasticity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Legacy ETS algorithm: override and goal seek (VBA)"}
- Row 1872 reads override prices from Manual inputs O15:AB15 (`OverrideOfETSPrices`); row 1873 uses them when the
  override switch is on.
- The full model computes covered emissions with the ETS (rows 1888-1953) and compares the actual reduction with the
  cap (rows 1956-1963: actual, cap, difference, ratio, error per year; maximum error in J1963).
- The workbook proposes a corrected price per year (`PricesAdjustedByErrorFactor`):
  $p \times$ (target log-reduction / actual log-reduction)$^{0.5}$ (convergence factor 0.5, row 1966).
- `OverrideETSFast` switches the ETS and the override on and calls `SolveFast`, a damped fixed-point iteration in
  log space:
  1. if StartFresh, seed the override row from the quick estimate;
  2. step $p \leftarrow p\,(r/p)^{\alpha}$, with $r$ the workbook's proposal;
  3. Anderson-style mixing: 0.7 new + 0.3 previous iterate;
  4. smoothing: 5% weight on a centred 3-year moving average;
  5. negative or invalid values keep the old price;
  6. write back, recalculate, take the worst-year error over all 14 years (the named `WorstYearlyETSError` averages
     only 9 years, so the macro bypasses it);
  7. halve $\alpha$ if the error got worse (minimum 0.0625); multiply it by 1.2 if the error more than halved
     (maximum 1);
  8. stop when the worst error is below `ETSErrorTolerance` or after `ETSMaxIterations`.
- The cached run has override prices of about 22-28 USD per t for 2028-2038, with jumps (1.5 in 2027, 13.8 in 2040)
  and a maximum error of 0.33. It had not converged; the cap rows are 0 in the cached state.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Legacy ETS algorithm: split of the price"}
The same split is used in both parts of the legacy model:

| Part | Legacy rows | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Auctioned | 1875-1879, 2252 (`egy.mit.etstraj`) | $p \times a$ enters fuel prices as a **price wedge**, like a carbon tax: fuel switching, efficiency and usage all respond. It raises revenue. |
| OBA / OBR | 1881-1885, 2343-2349 ("Feebate plus non-auctioned ETS"), 2402-2419 | $p \times (1 - a)$ enters as a **shadow price on the efficiency margin only**, like a feebate: no pass-through to consumer prices, no revenue. |

The legacy note on rows 1875-1885 says "Arguably this should be an exp/ln function TBC": the split is linear in $p$.
This is also why the OBA effectiveness is 0.5: only the efficiency share of the response is triggered, about half of
the total with the default elasticities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Design note: benchmarks instead of one auction share"}
This note records the design proposed for the model's ETS. Today the model uses legacy's one auctioned share per
scenario (LD7); the benchmark-based design below is the intended extension. Everything after the split stays as in
the legacy split.

- **Inputs** per subsector: the covered flag and a benchmark path $b(t)$, a share of the subsector's base-year
  emission intensity (for example 0.9: free allocation at 90% of base-year intensity; a declining path tightens it).
- **Shares.** Free allocation $FA = b \times$ base-year intensity $\times$ output, with output proxied by baseline
  fuel use (the model has no output variable). OBR share $s = \min(FA / \text{covered emissions}, 1)$; auctioned
  share $a = 1 - s$. To first order $s \approx b$ (intensity unchanged). Using actual covered emissions would be
  circular through fuel use, so the recommendation is scenario-1 (baseline) covered emissions (option A of the cap
  design note); $s$ is then a data-driven input.
- **Then as legacy.** Effectiveness $e = a + 0.5\, s$ per subsector; the auctioned part $p \times a$ is a price
  wedge (revenue = $p \times$ (covered emissions − FA)); the OBR part $p \times s$ joins the sector shadow price (the
  feebate channel); the fast estimate $p$ = (reduction left for the ETS) / $(\varepsilon\, e)$, with $\varepsilon$
  and $e$ weighted by covered baseline emissions.
- **Override.** An offline goal seek (a Python script with the same damped log-space step) writes a row of prices
  to paste. No VBA and no circular reference.

Without benchmarks the ETS is fully effective (permit price = carbon price path $\times$ coverage, as effective as a
carbon tax, per an earlier user decision), and the auction share only affects revenue. With benchmarks, the OBR part
moves from the price wedge to the shadow price, so emissions fall less for the same $p$, and revenue falls. A
benchmark of 0 (full auctioning) reproduces the fully effective case exactly.

**Open points.**

1. The fast estimate uses legacy's sector semi-elasticities. The model could derive them from its own elasticities
   (a one-off calibration run) to keep them consistent.
2. Legacy's linear split ($p \times a$) against a log form (legacy's own TBC note).
3. Legacy's relative price 1.1 (auctioned ETS against tax) and the risk-premium inputs (rows 1811-1813) are not used
   by the legacy fast estimate as cached; the model uses them through $V$ (LD8).
4. The CBAM sector semi-elasticity (−0.001) is not modelled.
:::
